title: Muni Kids Turns 11. The Muni Never Left.
cardDesc: Brothers Maxton and Drew Reinland started Muni Kids in Portland in 2015 because nobody was making golf gear for the people who actually learned the game on public courses. title: 8 Bucket Hats Worth the Brim
cardDesc: The bucket hat is having its quiet moment on the course — no logos screaming from the crown, no performance fabric monologues on the hang tag. title: Agronomy Workshop — A Golf Shirt with a Hidden Tee Slot and Nothing to Prove
cardDesc: Rob Junge designed exactly one shirt, put a hidden tee holder in the chest pocket, and called it a golf brand. The mock neck heavyweight work shirt — 17.5 oz cotton, made in LA — is the kind of garment that makes you wonder why anyone ever thought polyester was the answer to anything. The hats come with a pencil holder and an actual pencil, because this is the rare brand that remembers you need to write things down on a golf course. title: Late Nine — Stockholm, Relaxed Fits, and the Quiet Part of Golf
cardDesc: Founded in Stockholm in 2024, Late Nine makes golf clothes for people who think most golf clothes try too hard. Ribbed knits, pleated trousers, windbreakers — all cut relaxed, all made in small European factories that care about hand feel more than moisture-wicking stats. The references are late-'90s and early-2000s, back when golf showed up in film and nobody had to explain why it was cool. They use deadstock materials when they can, keep production runs limited, and price accordingly — polos from $252, outerwear north of $500. Not cheap, but you're paying for fabric choices made by people who clearly spend more time touching swatches than reading trend reports.

title: Fyfe Golf — Between Tides. Sail cloth, marine suede, and waxed canvas, made in Scotland.
cardDesc: Fyfe's new collection is built around the tidal window that lets you cross from mainland to links on the Scottish islands.
